sections.title: The bomber, the psychiatrist and the suit
sections.intro_md:
Just before midnight on 21 January 1957, four New York detectives knocked on a door at 17 Fourth Street, Waterbury, Connecticut. The man who answered, George Metesky, had planted at least 33 bombs across New York over 16 years. The story told ever since is that a psychiatrist, **James Brussel**, had described him in advance, right down to the clothes he would wear: a double-breasted suit, buttoned.

That story launched a profession. It is also the best place to see the problem with it. Brussel's profile was printed in the newspapers on 25 December 1956, and Metesky read the papers. Several of Brussel's guesses were wrong, and his 1968 memoir quietly left them out. And the bomber was not found by psychology at all. He was found by a clerk reading old files.

This day is about that gap: between how profiling is remembered and what the evidence says it can do.

spotlights.name: George Metesky, the Mad Bomber
spotlights.spot_it: Pipe bombs carried in wool socks, letters in block capitals signed F.P.
spotlights.story_md: Between 1940 and 1956 Metesky planted at least 33 bombs in New York, 22 of which exploded and injured 15 people. He hit Grand Central Terminal five times, Penn Station five times and Radio City Music Hall three times, and slit cinema seats to hide bombs in the stuffing. His grudge dated to 5 September 1931, when a boiler blast at Con Edison's Hell Gate plant left him gassed and, he said, cheated of compensation. He paused for the Second World War 'for patriotic reasons'. Asked what F.P. meant, he told detectives: 'Fair Play.' Judged insane, he was committed to Matteawan hospital in April 1957 and freed in December 1973.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The case every history of profiling begins with.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixteen years, 33 bombs, one workplace grudge: Fair Play.

spotlights.name: Brussel's profile, and what he left out
spotlights.spot_it: A list of confident guesses, printed in the New York Times under '16-Year Search for a Madman'.
spotlights.story_md: Psychiatrist James Brussel studied the letters and bomb photos and predicted a paranoid man, 40 to 50, neat, a model employee and a present or former Con Edison worker. Police published the profile on 25 December 1956, hoping errors would provoke the bomber into writing back. In his 1968 book, Casebook of a Crime Psychiatrist, Brussel recalled also calling a Slav from Connecticut in a buttoned double-breasted suit. The literary scholar Donald Foster, and later Malcolm Gladwell, checked the record: Brussel had actually told police to look for a man 'born and educated in Germany', living in White Plains, with a facial scar and a night job. Metesky was 53, born in Waterbury to Lithuanian parents, and largely unemployed. Gladwell compared the method to cold reading.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Remembering hits and forgetting misses is how a weak method acquires a strong reputation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Count the misses, not just the suit.

spotlights.name: Alice Kelly, the clerk who found him
spotlights.spot_it: Not a psychiatrist: a Con Edison clerk working through workers' compensation files.
spotlights.story_md: While the profile ran in the papers, Con Edison clerk Alice Kelly was searching the company's compensation files for former employees with serious health problems. On Friday 18 January 1957, in the last batch, she found a file marked 'injustice' and 'permanent disability', words the bomber had used in letters to the New York Journal-American. Metesky's own letters in the file used the phrase 'dastardly deeds'. Police first credited a detective. A later reward inquiry conceded that Kelly had found the file. She declined the $26,000 reward, saying she had only been doing her job.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The real break came from records and wording, not from a personality sketch.
spotlights.memory_hook: The bomber was caught by a filing clerk and his own favourite phrase.

sections.title: What a profile claims to do
sections.intro_md:
An offender profile is a set of predictions about an unknown offender, drawn from the crime itself: age range, sex, likely job, whether he lives alone, whether he has a record, how he will behave when questioned. The FBI calls its version **criminal investigative analysis**. Britain now calls the job **behavioural investigative adviser**.

There are four main schools. The FBI's crime-scene approach sorts crimes into types. Clinical profiling is a psychiatrist's reading of one case. **Investigative psychology**, founded by David Canter, uses statistics on solved cases. **Geographic profiling** predicts where an offender is based, not who he is.

All the personality-based versions rest on two assumptions. **Consistency**: an offender behaves similarly across his crimes. **Homology**: offenders who commit crimes in similar ways have similar backgrounds. The first holds up reasonably well. The second, as later sections show, mostly does not.

One warning about words: offender profiling is not racial profiling. The first works backwards from a crime to a person. The second stops people because of who they look like.

spotlights.name: Quantico and the job that does not exist
spotlights.spot_it: Brick buildings in Virginia woods, inside a Marine Corps base: the FBI Academy.
spotlights.story_md: The FBI Academy opened at Quantico, Virginia, on 7 May 1972. That year, after J. Edgar Hoover's death, Howard Teten and Patrick Mullany formed the Behavioral Science Unit. It grew into the National Center for the Analysis of Violent Crime in 1984, home to five Behavioral Analysis Units: one for terrorism, arson and bombing, one for threats, cyber crime and corruption, one for crimes against children, and others. Yet the FBI's own FAQ says: 'The FBI does not have a job called Profiler.' Supervisory special agents do the work, and, the FAQ adds, they 'do not get vibes or experience psychic flashes' at crime scenes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The real unit is smaller, slower and more bureaucratic than the television version.
spotlights.memory_hook: No vibes, no flashes, no job title: just supervisory special agents.

spotlights.name: The other profiling: stops by appearance
spotlights.spot_it: Same word, opposite direction: suspicion before any crime, based on group traits.
spotlights.story_md: Racial profiling means treating people as suspects because of race, religion or origin rather than evidence. In New York, the police stop-and-frisk programme led to Floyd v. City of New York. On 12 August 2013, Judge Shira Scheindlin ruled that the NYPD had violated the Fourth Amendment through unreasonable searches and the Fourteenth by stopping people in a racially discriminatory way. The two kinds of profiling share a weakness: both turn a statistical pattern into suspicion of one individual. India has its own long version of this, the colonial 'criminal tribes', covered later today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Keeping the two meanings apart prevents a lot of confused argument.
spotlights.memory_hook: Offender profiling starts at the crime; racial profiling starts at the face.

sections.title: Before the FBI: skulls, cards and a police surgeon
sections.intro_md:
The wish to read a criminal from the outside is old. In the 1870s the Italian doctor **Cesare Lombroso** said born criminals carried physical marks: odd ears, sloping foreheads, asymmetric faces. He was wrong, and his error is worth remembering, because it is the same leap profiling makes in a subtler form: from a visible pattern to a hidden nature.

In Paris, **Alphonse Bertillon** had a more modest goal. He did not try to explain criminals, only to recognise them again, using body measurements and standard photographs. His mug shot survives in every police station.

The first real profile came from a London police surgeon, **Thomas Bond**, in November 1888, during the Jack the Ripper murders. Berlin's murder squad under **Ernst Gennat** studied serial killers in the 1920s and 1930s. And in 1943 the American spy agency OSS paid a psychoanalyst, **Walter Langer**, to predict what Hitler would do if he lost the war.

spotlights.name: Cesare Lombroso and the 'born criminal'
spotlights.spot_it: A 19th-century doctor measuring skulls, convinced crime was written on the body.
spotlights.story_md: Lombroso (1835 to 1909), an army surgeon turned professor in Turin, published L'uomo delinquente in 1876. He argued that many criminals were 'atavistic', throwbacks to an earlier stage of evolution, recognisable by physical traits such as facial asymmetry, unusual ears and eye defects. His methods were descriptive: careful skull measurements, but no rigorous comparison with non-criminals. After he died, his own skull and brain were measured too. Criminologists abandoned his theory, but its shape survives wherever someone claims to read a dangerous person from surface signs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first scientific-sounding attempt to infer criminality from appearance, and a warning.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lombroso read crime in ears; profilers read it in crime scenes. Both need proof.

spotlights.name: Alphonse Bertillon and the mug shot
spotlights.spot_it: Front and side photographs on a card with body measurements: the Bertillon card.
spotlights.story_md: Bertillon (1853 to 1914) started as a copyist at the Paris Prefecture of Police in 1879. He built 'anthropometry', recording measurements such as head length and ear size so a repeat offender could be recognised under a new name. In 1888 he standardised police photography: one face-on picture and one profile, the mug shot. Fingerprints soon replaced his measurements. The difference from profiling matters. Bertillon only claimed to re-identify a known person from his body. He never claimed to deduce an unknown person's character from a crime.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Identification is a modest, testable claim; profiling's claims are larger.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bertillon measured to recognise, not to read minds.

spotlights.name: Thomas Bond's Ripper profile, 1888
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian surgeon's numbered memo about a killer nobody had seen.
spotlights.story_md: On 25 October 1888 Robert Anderson of Scotland Yard asked police surgeon Thomas Bond for his 'opinion on the matter'. Bond had examined Mary Jane Kelly's body and read the inquest notes on four earlier victims. His report of 10 November 1888 judged that the killer had no anatomical skill, not even a butcher's or horse slaughterer's, worked alone, was a man 'of physical strength and of great coolness and daring', and was probably 'solitary and eccentric', without regular work but with a small income, living among people who might suspect him. The Ripper was never caught, so the profile was never tested. Bond himself died in 1901.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Often called the first offender profile; also the first untestable one.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first profile described a man nobody ever found.

spotlights.name: Ernst Gennat, Berlin's murder detective
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy-set Berlin police chief who built the first standing homicide squad.
spotlights.story_md: Gennat (1880 to 1939) joined the Berlin police in 1904. There was no permanent homicide department, only an on-call service from 1902; Gennat pushed until one was created. His cases included the serial killers Fritz Haarmann and Peter Kurten. In 1930 he used the German word Serienmorder, serial murderer, decades before Robert Ressler popularised 'serial killer' in English. Gennat kept systematic files on murders and their methods, an early version of the case databases that later replaced intuition in the best profiling work.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Serial murder was studied as a pattern long before Quantico.
spotlights.memory_hook: 'Serial killer' was German before it was American.

spotlights.name: Walter Langer's report on Hitler
spotlights.spot_it: A secret 1943 psychoanalytic report predicting how Hitler would react to defeat.
spotlights.story_md: Walter Langer, a Harvard-trained psychoanalyst who had studied under Anna Freud in Vienna, was hired by the Office of Strategic Services. His 1943 analysis judged that suicide was the 'most plausible outcome' if Hitler faced defeat, and raised the possibility of a military coup well before the July 1944 plot. Hitler shot himself in April 1945. The report was published in 1972 as The Mind of Adolf Hitler. Later presidents asked for the same: Kennedy wanted a profile of Khrushchev before the 1961 Vienna summit. It shows the trap: one striking hit, built on Freudian theory that cannot be tested, is remembered far more than the rest of the document.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Profiling began as wartime psychoanalysis, a theory with little testable content.
spotlights.memory_hook: A spy agency paid a Freudian to predict Hitler's death, and he got one big call right.

sections.title: The Quantico years
sections.intro_md:
Modern profiling was built by a handful of FBI instructors in the 1970s. **Howard Teten** taught an 'Applied Criminology' class where police brought unsolved cases; with **Patrick Mullany** he formed the Behavioral Science Unit in 1972. Its first big test came in Montana in 1973.

From 1978 **Robert Ressler** and **John Douglas** began visiting prisons to interview convicted killers: Ed Kemper, Ted Bundy, Charles Manson, David Berkowitz and others, 36 in all. A nurse researcher, **Ann Burgess**, helped turn the conversations into data, and the work became the 1988 book Sexual Homicide. **Roy Hazelwood** supplied the most famous idea to come out of the unit: the split between 'organized' and 'disorganized' killers.

The interviews were real and often useful for understanding offenders. The problem was what came next: a small, unrepresentative sample of talkative convicts became the template for predicting unknown ones.

spotlights.name: The first FBI profile: Montana, 1973
spotlights.spot_it: A child taken from a family tent, a ransom call, and two FBI instructors writing guesses on paper.
spotlights.story_md: On 25 June 1973 seven-year-old Susan Jaeger was taken from her family's tent at Missouri Headwaters State Park. Teten and Mullany profiled a local white man, a loner with military service, and predicted he would call the family on the anniversary. On 25 June 1974 the kidnapper did call. Suspect David Meirhofer, a Vietnam veteran and carpenter, had been questioned under sodium pentothal and given a polygraph, which was inconclusive, and he was released. In September 1974 the FBI recorded another call, identified his voice and arrested him. Searchers found human remains at his home. He confessed to four murders and killed himself in his cell on 29 September 1974.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Profiling's founding success, and a reminder that the 'truth serum' and polygraph failed.
spotlights.memory_hook: The profile predicted the anniversary call; the tape recorder caught him.

spotlights.name: Robert Ressler
spotlights.spot_it: The Chicago-born agent who popularised 'serial killer' and co-founded ViCAP.
spotlights.story_md: Ressler (1937 to 2013) joined the FBI in 1970 and the Behavioral Science Unit soon after. With John Douglas he organised the prison interviews of 36 offenders. With retired LAPD detective Pierce Brooks he set up ViCAP, the Violent Criminal Apprehension Program, launched in 1985: a central database for linking unsolved violent crimes across police forces. He is often credited with coining 'serial killer', though Berlin's Ernst Gennat had used Serienmorder in 1930. In a lecture at Wichita State, Ressler guessed the BTK killer was a graduate in the criminal justice field. Dennis Rader had a 1979 Wichita State degree in administration of justice.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His most durable contribution was a database, not a typology.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ressler's best tool was a filing system for linking crimes.

spotlights.name: John Douglas, the original mindhunter
spotlights.spot_it: The ex-sniper and hostage negotiator whose memoir became a Netflix series.
spotlights.story_md: Douglas (born 1945) joined the FBI in 1970, served on a SWAT team as a sniper and as a hostage negotiator, and moved to the Behavioral Science Unit in 1977. He ran the profiling programme and interviewed Bundy, Manson, Kemper, Berkowitz and Gacy. His 1995 book Mindhunter, written with Mark Olshaker, became David Fincher's Netflix series in 2017. Douglas is not universally admired: in the Atlanta child murders he gave People magazine a profile of the killer as a young Black man, widely read as the FBI prejudging suspect Wayne Williams. At 80 he was still on the bill at CrimeCon in Las Vegas in May 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The public image of profiling is largely his.
spotlights.memory_hook: One agent's memoir taught the world what a profiler is.

spotlights.name: Roy Hazelwood
spotlights.spot_it: The sex-crimes specialist behind 'organized' and 'disorganized'.
spotlights.story_md: Hazelwood (1938 to 2016) was an army military police officer who served in Vietnam before joining the FBI in 1971. In 1980 he developed the distinction between organized and disorganized murderers and sorted rapists into six types, from 'power-reassurance' to 'anger-excitation'. He also took on 'equivocal death analysis', judging whether an unclear death was suicide, accident or murder. That led to his most criticised case: in 1989, with Richard Ault, he concluded that sailor Clayton Hartwig had probably caused the USS Iowa explosion. Ten of 14 psychologists asked by Congress later rejected that analysis.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His typologies still shape police training, despite weak empirical support.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two neat boxes, organized and disorganized, came from one agent's case experience.

spotlights.name: Ann Burgess, the nurse who brought data
spotlights.spot_it: A psychiatric nurse at a computer in a room of FBI men.
spotlights.story_md: Ann Wolbert Burgess (born 1936) made her name studying rape victims in 1970s Boston and helped define rape trauma. The FBI brought her in to help code the prison interviews into a research database, and she co-wrote Sexual Homicide (1988) with Ressler and Douglas, and the Crime Classification Manual. She once arrived to interview victims of a serial rapist and local police phoned the FBI to check, assuming a woman claiming to work with the Bureau was an impostor. The Mindhunter character Wendy Carr is loosely based on her, and Hulu's 2024 documentary Mastermind: To Think Like a Killer tells her story.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She pushed profiling toward systematic data, its most defensible direction.
spotlights.memory_hook: The FBI's mindhunters needed a nurse with a spreadsheet.

spotlights.name: Ed Kemper, the talkative interviewee
spotlights.spot_it: A very large, articulate killer who explained himself at length to FBI agents.
spotlights.story_md: Edmund Kemper killed his grandparents at 15, was released in 1969, and between May 1972 and April 1973 murdered seven women, including his mother, and one girl. Most of his victims were hitchhiking students near Santa Cruz; he had a university parking sticker from his mother's job, so women trusted his car. Tested in custody, he scored an IQ of 136. Kemper became one of the FBI's most forthcoming interviewees, and Mindhunter cast him as the agents' first teacher. That is the catch: a profile built from killers who enjoy talking may describe talkers, not killers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The interview programme's star witness shows its sampling problem.
spotlights.memory_hook: The FBI learned most from the killers who loved an audience.

sections.title: Organized or disorganized?
sections.intro_md:
In April 1980 the FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin published 'The Lust Murderer', introducing two kinds of sexual killer. The **organized** offender plans, brings a weapon and takes it away, controls the victim and leaves little evidence; the theory says he is intelligent, socially competent and employed. The **disorganized** offender acts on impulse, leaves a chaotic scene and evidence behind; he is said to be a loner of low intelligence who lives near the scene. A 'mixed' category followed in 1985.

The appeal is obvious. Look at the scene, pick a box, read off the person. The typology spread into training courses, textbooks and even murder trials.

The trouble is that it was built from the interview sample, not tested on fresh data. When psychologists finally ran the numbers, the two boxes did not appear.

data.organized: Features common to most serial killings
data.disorganized: Rare, and not a distinct type

spotlights.name: The organized/disorganized dichotomy
spotlights.spot_it: Two boxes for every killer: the planner and the chaotic one.
spotlights.story_md: Credited to Roy Hazelwood and built on the BSU interviews, the dichotomy was described in the April 1980 FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin, extended with a 'mixed' type in August 1985, and set out in Sexual Homicide in 1988. The interviews behind it were informal and ad hoc: 36 convicted offenders who agreed to talk, with no comparison group of non-offenders and no check on how honestly they described themselves. Critics note that real scenes are usually a mixture, and that the categories describe the crime more than the person. Even so, the two labels became the most widely used typology in profiling.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A convenient story became a standard tool before anyone tested it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two boxes, 36 talkers, no control group.

spotlights.name: The 2004 test: 100 killers, no two types
spotlights.spot_it: A statistical map of crime-scene features that should have split into two clusters, and did not.
spotlights.story_md: David Canter and colleagues at Liverpool coded 39 crime-scene features from 100 murders by 100 different US serial killers and used multidimensional scaling to see which features occur together. If the dichotomy were real, the organized features should cluster on one side and the disorganized ones on the other. They did not. Organized features turned out to be typical of most serial killings, so they cannot tell offenders apart. Disorganized features were much rarer and did not form a distinct type. The paper, in Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, was titled 'Myth or model?' Its answer leaned towards myth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous profiling typology failed its first serious statistical test.
spotlights.memory_hook: Most killers look 'organized', so the label tells you almost nothing.

sections.title: Putting profilers to the test
sections.intro_md:
How would you know if profilers are good? The cleanest test is to give everyone the same solved case and score their predictions against the real offender. Since 1990 researchers have done exactly that, pitting professional profilers against detectives, psychologists, students and, in one famous study, self-declared psychics.

The results are awkward for both sides. Profilers usually write longer profiles and sometimes do a bit better. But the gap is small, inconsistent between cases, and often matched by people with no investigative experience at all. Science students did well; experienced detectives often did not. The researchers who ran the best-known experiments disagree fiercely with each other about what the numbers mean.

A 2007 review of 130 profiling articles found that most relied on common sense, and that 60% used at least one anecdote as evidence. Its meta-analysis is charted below.

spotlights.name: Pinizzotto and Finkel, 1990
spotlights.spot_it: Five groups, two solved cases, one question: who predicts the offender best?
spotlights.story_md: Anthony Pinizzotto and Norman Finkel of Georgetown University gave detailed case files from two solved crimes, a murder and a rape, to five groups: FBI profilers, detectives trained by the FBI, other detectives, clinical psychologists and students. Each wrote a profile, which was scored against the convicted offender. The profilers wrote longer, more detailed profiles, and on the rape case they got more details right than any other group. On the murder case they did no better on average than the non-profilers. Critics later pointed out that, counted as a share of each profile's statements, the students scored as well as or better than the profilers on both cases. The study, in Law and Human Behavior, became the template for every later test.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first controlled test found an edge that appeared in one case and vanished in the other.
spotlights.memory_hook: Better on the rape, no better on the murder.

spotlights.name: Kocsis and the psychics
spotlights.spot_it: Profilers, police, psychologists, students and psychics, all profiling the same solved crime.
spotlights.story_md: Australian psychologist Richard Kocsis ran a series of studies from 2000 using solved arson and murder cases. Groups included professional profilers, science students, psychologists, police recruits, experienced officers, arson investigators and self-declared psychics. Profilers made the most correct predictions, but also varied the most: some were very good, some poor. Science students, chosen for their logical reasoning, did comparatively well and in some tests beat experienced police. Kocsis concluded that investigative experience mattered less than logic. The psychics appeared to rely on a social stereotype of a murderer. Critics such as Craig Bennell and Brent Snook argued in 2006 that Kocsis's scoring method flattered the profilers, and the dispute was never settled.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Even the most supportive studies show only a modest, uneven edge.
spotlights.memory_hook: Students with good logic beat detectives with years on the job.

spotlights.name: The 2007 meta-analysis
spotlights.spot_it: 130 articles reviewed; profilers' advantage measured in correlation coefficients.
spotlights.story_md: Brent Snook and colleagues pooled the accuracy studies. In their first analysis, profilers and experienced investigators were slightly better than comparison groups at an overall description (r = .24) and physical traits (r = .10), but no better at offence behaviour (r = .00) and slightly worse on thought processes and social history. The confidence intervals were so wide that the estimates were judged imprecise. Many 'correct' predictions were things anyone could guess about serial offenders: age range, previous convictions, substance use. The authors concluded that, until reproducible studies show otherwise, profiling looks like 'an extraneous and redundant pseudoscientific technique'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best summary of the evidence found little reliable advantage.
spotlights.memory_hook: r = .24 on a good day, zero on behaviour.

sections.title: Why profiles feel accurate
sections.intro_md:
If the accuracy evidence is so thin, why do surveys keep finding that police like profiles? In Britain in 1995, 82.6% of 184 officers said profiling advice was operationally useful and 92.4% said they would use it again, yet it rarely identified the offender directly.

Psychologists point to three mechanisms. First, **vagueness**: many profile statements are so general they fit almost anyone, the same trick that makes horoscopes feel personal. Second, **selective counting**: published case studies report the hits and forget the misses. Third, **authority**: officers rate the same profile as more accurate when told it came from an expert.

None of this means profilers are frauds. It means a profile can feel right even when it is not, and that feeling is not evidence.

data.note: from 21 profiles used in major cases

spotlights.name: Forer's horoscope trick and the Barnum effect
spotlights.spot_it: A personality reading that everyone in the class thinks was written for them.
spotlights.story_md: In 1948 psychologist Bertram Forer gave 39 students a personality test, then handed each a 'personal' description: 'You have a great need for other people to like and admire you... At times you are extroverted, affable, sociable, while at other times you are introverted, wary, reserved.' Students rated its accuracy 4.30 out of 5. Every student had the same text, assembled from a newsstand astrology book. Paul Meehl named it the Barnum effect in 1956, after the showman P. T. Barnum. Profiles full of statements like 'he may have had problems with women' or 'he has a troubled relationship with authority' work the same way.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Vague statements feel specific when you already believe they are about you.
spotlights.memory_hook: If it fits everyone, it identifies no one.

spotlights.name: One profile, two different killers
spotlights.spot_it: Two groups of detectives, the same profile, different 'real' offenders. Both said it fitted.
spotlights.story_md: Laurence Alison and colleagues gave police officers a genuine profile from a murder case. One group then read a description of the real offender. The other read a fabricated offender, substantially different. Asked how accurate the profile was, both groups gave it about 5.3 out of 7. In a companion study the team broke 21 profiles used in British and American investigations into 3,090 statements. Of 880 predictions about the offender, 82% came with no reasoning, 55% could never be checked and only 28% were specific enough to be proved wrong.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Once someone is arrested, almost any profile looks as if it described him.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same profile, different man, same score: 5.3 out of 7.

spotlights.name: The profile that was 38% right
spotlights.spot_it: A celebrated FBI case study, re-scored by counting every prediction.
spotlights.story_md: In 1986 Douglas, Ressler, Burgess and Hartman published a case study showing how well a profile had matched the offender. The profile made 29 predictions. The article highlighted the correct ones. When Snook and colleagues counted, there were 11 correct calls (10 hits and one correct rejection) and 18 wrong ones. That is 38% accuracy: fewer than half the predictions were right. The lesson is not that this profile was unusually bad, but that the way success stories are told hides the denominator.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without the misses, every profile is a triumph.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eleven right, eighteen wrong, reported as a success.

sections.title: The person and the situation
sections.intro_md:
Underneath the accuracy studies is a deeper scientific problem. Classic profiling assumes that behaviour flows mainly from stable personality traits: an organized personality makes an organized crime scene. Personality psychology has doubted that since 1968, when **Walter Mischel** showed that behaviour across situations is far less consistent than trait theories assumed. What people do depends heavily on the situation: a victim who fights back, a neighbour's light coming on, alcohol, panic.

The second blow is to homology, the idea that similar crimes mean similar offenders. When researchers tested it directly on rapists, offenders whose crimes looked alike were not more alike in age, job or criminal record.

What does survive is narrower. An offender's own crimes often resemble each other enough to link a series, and where he commits them says a lot about where he lives. Those two findings are the basis of the better methods later in this day.

spotlights.name: Walter Mischel and the consistency problem
spotlights.spot_it: The psychologist famous for the marshmallow test, and for a 1968 book that shook personality theory.
spotlights.story_md: Walter Mischel's 1968 book Personality and Assessment reviewed decades of studies and found that the core assumption of trait theory, that a person behaves consistently across different situations, was often not supported. Mischel did not say personality is meaningless. He argued that consistency appears as stable 'if this situation, then that behaviour' patterns. For profiling this is a direct challenge: a single crime is one situation, often chaotic and brief, and reading a whole personality from it is exactly the inference his work warned against.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Profiling's personality model is the one psychology moved away from decades ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: One crime is one situation, not a whole person.

spotlights.name: Testing homology: similar crimes, different men
spotlights.spot_it: Pairs of rapes that look alike, committed by men who do not.
spotlights.story_md: In 2002 Andreas Mokros and Laurence Alison took a sample of convicted rapists and compared how similar their crimes were with how similar the men were. If homology held, offenders with similar crime-scene behaviour should also be similar in age, occupation and criminal history. There was no significant relationship. A related review by Alison, Bennell, Mokros and Ormerod concluded that predicting demographic features from behaviour in 'short-term, highly traumatic situations seems an overly ambitious and unlikely possibility', and that such claims 'should be entirely excluded from consideration in court' until verified.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The core inference of personality profiling failed when measured.
spotlights.memory_hook: Crimes that look alike do not mean men who look alike.

sections.title: When the profile pointed the wrong way
sections.intro_md:
A weak profile that is ignored does little harm. The danger comes when investigators believe it. Then it can do two kinds of damage: it can fix attention on an innocent person who 'fits', and it can steer a hunt away from the real offender who does not.

The five cases below are not a random sample of profiling, and many profiles in other cases were harmless or mildly helpful. But they show the specific mechanisms of failure again and again: **tunnel vision**, where the profile becomes the theory to be proved; **trait filters**, where real suspects are eliminated because they do not match a guessed height, accent or race; and **psychological autopsies** of dead people who cannot answer back.

In several of these cases the profile was only one ingredient. Pressure from the press, the public and senior officers did the rest.

pins.label: USS Iowa explosion, near Puerto Rico, 1989

spotlights.name: Rachel Nickell and the honeytrap
spotlights.spot_it: A profile, an undercover officer posing as a lonely heart, and a case thrown out at the Old Bailey.
spotlights.story_md: On 15 July 1992 Rachel Nickell, 23, was stabbed 49 times on Wimbledon Common in front of her two-year-old son. With no forensic link to local man Colin Stagg, police asked psychologist Paul Britton for a profile, decided Stagg fitted it, and ran Operation Edzell: for five months an undercover officer feigned romance and drew out his sexual fantasies. In September 1994 Mr Justice Ognall threw the evidence out as 'deceptive conduct of the grossest kind'. The real killer, Robert Napper, killed a mother and child in 1993 and admitted Nickell's manslaughter in 2008. Earlier, police had ruled Napper out of a rape series because he was over six feet tall. Stagg received £706,000.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The textbook case of a profile turning into a theory the police then tried to prove.
spotlights.memory_hook: The profile fitted the wrong man; a height filter freed the right one.

spotlights.name: Richard Jewell, the hero who 'fitted'
spotlights.spot_it: A security guard who found a bomb, then spent 88 days as the FBI's suspect.
spotlights.story_md: Just after midnight on 27 July 1996, security guard Richard Jewell spotted a green backpack under a bench at Atlanta's Centennial Olympic Park, alerted officers and helped clear the area before three pipe bombs exploded. One woman, Alice Hawthorne, was killed. Three days later the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that the FBI was treating Jewell as a suspect, based largely on a 'lone bomber' profile: a frustrated would-be policeman who plants a bomb so he can be the hero who finds it. He was cleared after 88 days. Eric Rudolph pleaded guilty in April 2005. Jewell died in 2007; Clint Eastwood's film followed in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A plausible-sounding type replaced evidence, and the press amplified it.
spotlights.memory_hook: He found the bomb, so the profile said he planted it.

spotlights.name: The Beltway snipers and the white van
spotlights.spot_it: Everyone looking for a white van and a lone white man; the killers were two Black men in a blue Caprice.
spotlights.story_md: Over three weeks in October 2002, ten people were killed and three wounded around Washington, D.C., each by a single long-range shot. Witnesses mentioned a white box truck or van, and commentators and profilers widely predicted a lone white male. The shooters were John Allen Muhammad, 41, an army veteran, and Lee Boyd Malvo, 17, firing through a hole cut in the trunk of a 1990 Chevrolet Caprice. Police had checked the Caprice's New Jersey plate near shooting scenes several times and even stopped it on 3 October, but let it go: the computers showed nothing and attention was on the van. A trucker's 911 call led to their arrest on 24 October.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Wrong assumptions about the offender filtered out the car that was in plain sight.
spotlights.memory_hook: Everyone hunted a white van; the killers drove a blue sedan.

spotlights.name: USS Iowa: profiling a dead sailor
spotlights.spot_it: A battleship turret explodes and the FBI writes a psychological autopsy blaming one of the dead.
spotlights.story_md: On 19 April 1989 the No. 2 gun turret of USS Iowa exploded, killing 47 men. The Navy's investigation concluded that gunner's mate Clayton Hartwig had done it deliberately, citing an FBI 'equivocal death analysis' by Richard Ault and Roy Hazelwood. Leaks smeared Hartwig and another sailor. Congress asked 14 psychologists from the American Psychological Association to review the analysis: ten rejected it, four found it plausible, and all 14 criticised the method. In 1991 Sandia National Laboratories and the GAO concluded the blast was probably an accidental 'overram' of powder bags. In October 1991 the Navy said it had found no evidence the blast was deliberate, and Admiral Frank Kelso offered Hartwig's family his 'sincere regrets'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A profile of a dead man filled the gap where physical evidence was missing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty-seven died; a profile blamed one of them; physics pointed to an accident.

spotlights.name: Wearside Jack and the Yorkshire Ripper
spotlights.spot_it: A taunting tape in a north-east accent that pulled a murder hunt towards Sunderland.
spotlights.story_md: Between March 1978 and June 1979 a hoaxer sent letters and a cassette to the Ripper inquiry, the tape saying: 'I'm Jack. I see you're having no luck catching me.' Detectives treated the Wearside accent as a profile of the killer, and the inquiry swung towards Sunderland. The real killer, Peter Sutcliffe, was a lorry driver from Bradford whom police interviewed nine times. He was caught on 2 January 1981 in Sheffield, stopped by chance for false number plates. The hoax may have delayed his arrest by 18 months. In 2005 DNA from an envelope identified the hoaxer, John Humble, who was jailed for eight years in 2006.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A single trait treated as a filter can eliminate the right man.
spotlights.memory_hook: One fake accent bought a real killer 18 months.

sections.title: What actually caught them
sections.intro_md:
Look at how famous serial offenders were really identified and a pattern appears. Hardly ever is it a personality profile. It is a traffic stop, a fibre, a filing clerk, a brother who recognised a turn of phrase, a floppy disk, a DNA match from a relative.

That does not make behavioural analysis useless. Linking crimes into a series, prioritising long suspect lists, planning interviews and choosing what to release to the media are real contributions, and the cases below include some. David Canter's 1986 profile of the Railway Rapist is still the strongest British example of a profile that helped.

But the honest summary, repeated in police reviews, is that profiles rarely name anyone. Forensic science, records and ordinary detective work do. Since 2018, genetic genealogy has solved cold cases that defeated every profiler who looked at them.

spotlights.name: The Railway Rapist: a profile that helped
spotlights.spot_it: A psychologist's 17 points that put a Kilburn railway carpenter near the top of the list.
spotlights.story_md: In 1985 and 1986 a man, sometimes with an accomplice, attacked women near railway stations around London, then murdered three, starting with Alison Day near Hackney Wick. Police brought in David Canter of the University of Surrey, the first use of a psychologist's offender profile in a major British investigation. Canter drew up 17 points about the attacker, including where he probably lived. John Duffy, a former railway carpenter from Kilburn, was arrested on 26 November 1986 and convicted in 1988. He fitted most of the 17 points: 13, by the usual count. Yet Canter saw the limits of what he had done, the subjective opinion of one psychologist, and set out to build investigative psychology on data rather than intuition.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best British success story, and its author drew the lesson of humility.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirteen of seventeen, and a psychologist who decided one opinion was not a method.

spotlights.name: The Unabomber: two profiles, both set aside
spotlights.spot_it: Seventeen years of mail bombs, and a brother who recognised a writing style.
spotlights.story_md: From 1978 to 1995 Ted Kaczynski's bombs killed three people and injured 23. In 1980 John Douglas's unit profiled the bomber as an intelligent man with links to academia. That profile was dropped in 1983 for a rival theory, built from bomb fragments, of a blue-collar airline mechanic. Neither identified him. In September 1995 the Washington Post published his 35,000-word manifesto. His brother David, urged by his wife, compared it with old family letters and recognised the phrasing. FBI agent James Fitzgerald's linguistic comparison supported the match, and Kaczynski was arrested at his Montana cabin in April 1996.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Family recognition and language analysis did what the profiles could not.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first profile was closer than its replacement, and neither caught him.

spotlights.name: Gary Ridgway, the Green River Killer
spotlights.spot_it: A truck painter interviewed early, released, and named by DNA 18 years later.
spotlights.story_md: The first known victim of the Green River Killer was found near Seattle in July 1982. Gary Ridgway, a painter at the Kenworth truck plant, became a suspect in 1983 and was interviewed. In April 1987 police took hair and saliva samples from him. Only when DNA techniques improved did the samples link him to the victims, and he was arrested at the factory on 30 November 2001. He confessed to 48 murders, more confirmed murders than any other American serial killer. A special spray paint on a victim's clothing that could have pointed to him was not tested for 20 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The decisive evidence was collected in 1987 and read in 2001.
spotlights.memory_hook: The decisive sample was taken in 1987 and read in 2001.

spotlights.name: BTK's floppy disk
spotlights.spot_it: A purple 1.44-megabyte Memorex disk mailed to a Wichita TV station.
spotlights.story_md: Dennis Rader killed ten people in and around Wichita between 1974 and 1991 and taunted police by letter as BTK, 'bind, torture, kill'. In 2004 he resumed writing. He asked police whether a floppy disk could be traced, and they answered with a classified ad in the Wichita Eagle: 'Rex, it will be ok.' On 16 February 2005 he mailed a disk to KSAS-TV. A deleted Word file on it carried the metadata 'Christ Lutheran Church' and 'last modified by Dennis'. An internet search showed that a Dennis Rader was president of the church council. A black Jeep Cherokee was parked outside his house, matching surveillance footage. He was arrested within days.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Digital forensics, plus police deception, ended a 30-year case.
spotlights.memory_hook: A killer asked the police a tech question, and believed the answer.

spotlights.name: The Golden State Killer and genetic genealogy
spotlights.spot_it: Decades of sketches and profiles, then a family tree built from a crime-scene DNA sample.
spotlights.story_md: Between the mid-1970s and 1986 one man committed more than 50 rapes and at least 13 murders across California, under names such as the East Area Rapist and the Original Night Stalker. In 2001 DNA showed these were one offender, but no database held his profile. In 2018 investigators uploaded crime-scene DNA to a public genealogy service, found distant relatives, and built family trees until one name fitted: Joseph James DeAngelo, a former police officer, arrested on 24 April 2018. He pleaded guilty on 29 June 2020. The method has since been used in many other cold cases, and raised its own privacy questions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A new forensic technique outperformed four decades of behavioural guesswork.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not his personality: his cousins.

sections.title: Better methods: maps, data and humility
sections.intro_md:
The most defensible parts of profiling make smaller claims. Instead of 'he is a socially inadequate loner who hates his mother', they say 'he probably lives in this two-square-kilometre area', 'these three attacks are probably by one man', or 'offenders of this type usually already have a record for burglary'. Each of those can be checked against data.

**Geographic profiling**, developed by Vancouver police officer **Kim Rossmo**, uses the fact that most offenders strike close to home but not too close. **Investigative psychology**, founded by **David Canter**, uses statistics from solved cases rather than case anecdotes. A 2018 review of 426 studies by Bryanna Fox and David Farrington found the research becoming more rigorous, with more statistical methods, though still thin on whether profiles help solve cases.

Britain shows the professional version and its fragility: by the 2020s only two full-time behavioural investigative advisers served all of the country's police forces.

spotlights.name: Kim Rossmo, the policeman with a map
spotlights.spot_it: A Vancouver detective who turned 'where' into an algorithm.
spotlights.story_md: Rossmo joined Vancouver police as a civilian in 1978 and became an officer in 1980. In 1995 he became the first police officer in Canada to earn a doctorate in criminology, at Simon Fraser University, where geographic profiling grew out of research from 1989. His formula became the Rigel software. In 1998 his analysis of women missing from Vancouver's Downtown Eastside concluded that a serial killer was at work. Senior officers did not accept it; he left in 2001. Robert Pickton was arrested in 2002. Rossmo now holds a chair in criminology at Texas State University and has applied the method to bumblebees, invasive species and disease.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His best-known warning was ignored, and the killer kept killing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rossmo saw the pattern in 1998; the arrest came in 2002.

spotlights.name: Distance decay and the buffer zone
spotlights.spot_it: Crimes thin out with distance from home, except for a quiet ring right around it.
spotlights.story_md: Geographic profiling rests on environmental criminology. Offenders commit crimes where their routine paths cross opportunities, so crimes cluster near home, work or regular routes and become rarer further out: distance decay. Close to home there is often a buffer zone where they avoid offending in case neighbours recognise them. In 1993 Canter and Larkin split serial offenders into 'marauders', who strike around their base, and 'commuters', who travel to a separate hunting ground. Programs such as Rigel and CrimeStat turn crime coordinates into a 'jeopardy surface', a heat map that ranks where to look first. The output can be scored: how much of the map you search before reaching the offender's home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A geographic profile makes a testable, narrow prediction.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not too far from home, and not on the doorstep.

spotlights.name: David Canter and investigative psychology
spotlights.spot_it: A Liverpool psychologist who replaced the profiler's hunch with tables of solved cases.
spotlights.story_md: Canter, born in Liverpool in 1944, began as an environmental psychologist studying how people behave in buildings and fires. After the Railway Rapist case he coined 'investigative psychology' and argued for an 'A to C' science: measure which crime actions (A) really go with which offender characteristics (C) across many solved cases, rather than trusting one expert's reading. His group's 2004 test of the organized/disorganized typology came out of that programme. In later life he earned a PhD in music composition. Rival researchers such as Richard Kocsis accused his camp of promoting its own approach; the dispute is still argued in journals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made profiling a research question instead of a talent.
spotlights.memory_hook: From A to C, with the numbers in between.

spotlights.name: Britain's two behavioural advisers
spotlights.spot_it: The modern British 'profiler': an adviser to the senior investigator, not a detective.
spotlights.story_md: Since the late 1990s British profiling has been rebuilt with training, quality control and national coordination. Behavioural investigative advisers give senior investigating officers crime-scene assessments, rankings of hypotheses, linkage analysis between offences, predictive profiling of the likely offender, media advice and prioritisation matrices for suspect lists. They also help target familial DNA searches by predicting an offender's likely age and area, and so those of his relatives. A national policing case study reports that numbers have shrunk to two: Lee Rainbow, the UK's first full-time profiler from 1999, and Adam Gregory. Their own description: gone are the days of 'subjective, unsupported musings'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Profiling done carefully looks like decision support, not mind-reading.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two advisers for a whole country, and no psychic flashes.

sections.title: India: from 'criminal tribes' to brain scans
sections.intro_md:
India has lived through the most extreme form of profiling: an entire legal system built on the idea that some communities are born criminal. The **Criminal Tribes Act of 1871** let colonial officials 'notify' whole castes and tribes as criminal. By the most widely cited estimate, about 13 million people in 127 communities were on the lists by 1947, forced to register and carry passes. The Act was repealed in 1949 and the communities 'denotified' on 31 August 1952, but the Habitual Offenders Acts that followed kept much of the stigma alive. In October 2024 the Supreme Court struck down prison-manual rules that still treated denotified tribes as habitual offenders.

Indian policing also became a testing ground for 'scientific' interrogation: narcoanalysis, polygraphs and a home-grown brain test called **BEOS**. In 2010 the Supreme Court barred forcing them on anyone. BEOS is still in use.

Indian investigators have also borrowed the psychological autopsy, most visibly in the 2018 Burari deaths in Delhi.

spotlights.name: The Criminal Tribes Act, 1871
spotlights.spot_it: A colonial law that made birth into a community proof of criminality.
spotlights.story_md: Introducing the 1871 Act, the official usually named as T. V. Stephens told the legislature that 'tribes whose ancestors were criminals from time immemorial' were 'destined by the usage of caste to commit crime'. Once a community was notified, there was no appeal. Adult men had to report to the police weekly, movement needed passes, and in some regions children were separated from parents and families held in settlements without trial. The law drew on the Thuggee Act of 1836, which let people be convicted for membership of a 'thug' gang. Repeal came in August 1949. Today India lists 313 nomadic and 198 denotified tribes that still face suspicion from police, courts and the press.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The purest example of profiling: guilt assigned by group, not by deed.
spotlights.memory_hook: In 1871 the law decided who was a criminal at birth.

spotlights.name: Budhan Theatre and the death of Budhan Sabar
spotlights.spot_it: Young actors from Ahmedabad's Chharanagar re-enacting a custodial death on the street.
spotlights.story_md: In February 1998 Budhan Sabar, of the denotified Kheria Sabar community, was arrested for theft in Purulia, West Bengal, and was found hanged in custody days later. The writer Mahasweta Devi took up the case, wrote to the Calcutta High Court, and the CBI later charged the police officer in charge; a Purulia court convicted him in 2023. The same year as the death, Mahasweta Devi and the linguist G. N. Devy helped found Budhan Theatre among the Chhara, a denotified community in Ahmedabad. Its signature play, Budhan, re-enacts his death and demands justice. Several of its actors went on to the National School of Drama.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The people once profiled by law now answer back on stage.
spotlights.memory_hook: A community labelled criminal in 1871 turned its story into theatre.

spotlights.name: BEOS, India's brain-scan test
spotlights.spot_it: A suspect in an EEG headset listening to short sentences describing the crime.
spotlights.story_md: Brain Electrical Oscillation Signature profiling was developed around 2005 by psychologist C. R. Mukundan with the Directorate of Forensic Science in Gandhinagar. The suspect hears phrases such as 'I took a knife' while an EEG records brain activity, and software claims to detect 'experiential knowledge'. In 2008 a Pune court cited BEOS when sentencing Aditi Sharma to life for poisoning her former fiance; the Bombay High Court granted bail in 2009. A government panel of neuroscientists called its basis 'suboptimal' in 2008. A June 2025 investigation by Science found BEOS used in at least 700 cases, still influencing some bail decisions, though its main validation study, with 110 participants, was never peer reviewed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A test without independent validation is still steering real cases.
spotlights.memory_hook: A brain scan that reads 'experience', according to the company that sells it.

spotlights.name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka, 2010

where.label: Supreme Court of India, New Delhi

spotlights.spot_it: The Supreme Court judgment on narcoanalysis, polygraphs and brain mapping.
spotlights.story_md: On 5 May 2010 a three-judge bench led by Chief Justice K. G. Balakrishnan ruled that forcing a person to undergo narcoanalysis, a polygraph or the Brain Electrical Activation Profile test violates the right against self-incrimination in Article 20(3) and personal liberty in Article 21. The court called compulsory testing an unjustified intrusion into mental privacy. It noted that sodium pentothal does not reliably produce truth. Tests may still be done with consent, under National Human Rights Commission guidelines, and facts later discovered through them can be admitted. The ruling did not end the tests; it moved them to the consent form.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's top court put constitutional limits on 'truth machines'.
spotlights.memory_hook: No forced truth serum, no forced brain map.

spotlights.name: The Burari deaths and a psychological autopsy
spotlights.spot_it: Eleven members of one Delhi family found dead, and a report on their state of mind.
spotlights.story_md: On 1 July 2018 eleven members of the Chundawat family were found dead in their house in Burari, north Delhi, ten of them hanging. Delhi Police asked the CBI to carry out a psychological autopsy. Its Central Forensic Science Laboratory studied years of notes found in the house, police statements and interviews with relatives. The report, received on 12 September 2018, concluded the deaths were not suicide but 'an accident that occurred during the course of performing a ritual', and that none of the deceased intended to die. It is a reconstruction of minds that cannot be questioned, the same technique that went so wrong on USS Iowa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Psychological autopsies can be useful context, and cannot be checked against the dead.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eleven deaths, a diary and a report on intentions nobody can confirm.

spotlights.name: Sukanya Shantha v. Union of India, 2024

where.label: Supreme Court of India, New Delhi

spotlights.spot_it: A journalist's investigation that took caste out of prison rulebooks.
spotlights.story_md: Journalist Sukanya Shantha reported that state prison manuals still assigned work by caste and singled out people from denotified tribes. On 3 October 2024 a bench led by Chief Justice D. Y. Chandrachud struck those rules down. Manuals in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan had labelled members of 'wandering' or 'criminal' tribes as dangerous; the court held that treating denotified-tribe prisoners as habitual offenders violates dignity and personal liberty, and ordered the manuals revised. Seventy-two years after denotification, the old profile was still written into official rules.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Colonial profiling survived in the paperwork until 2024.
spotlights.memory_hook: Denotified in 1952, still listed in prison manuals in 2024.

sections.title: Profilers on screen
sections.intro_md:
Most people meet profiling through fiction, and fiction set the expectations real profilers then had to manage. Thomas Harris built Red Dragon (1981) and The Silence of the Lambs (1988) around an FBI unit that 'creates psychological profiles of serial killers'. The 1991 film made Clarice Starling and Hannibal Lecter household names. Criminal Minds has run since 2005, Mindhunter dramatised the founding years, and British drama Cracker gave television its own scruffy psychologist.

Screen profilers are brilliant, intuitive and nearly always right, and the drama comes from the leap of insight. Researchers have suggested this is part of why profiling stays popular despite the evidence: we enjoy the detective-genius story of Sherlock Holmes and Poirot, and real case studies are often told the same way. Real advisers spend most of their time reading files and ranking options.

spotlights.name: The Silence of the Lambs
spotlights.spot_it: An FBI trainee interviewing a caged psychiatrist to catch a serial killer.
spotlights.story_md: Thomas Harris's novel, published in 1988, sends trainee Clarice Starling to question Hannibal Lecter for help catching 'Buffalo Bill'. Her boss Jack Crawford heads the FBI division that profiles serial killers, a fictional version of the Behavioral Science Unit. Jonathan Demme's 1991 film won all five main Oscars, best picture, director, actor, actress and screenplay, and is still the only horror film to win best picture. Robert Ressler's memoir was later marketed as the true story of the detective behind the book. The film's image of profiling, a lone genius reading a killer's mind, is the one research keeps colliding with.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The single biggest source of the public's idea of a profiler.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five Oscars for the myth of the mind-reader.

spotlights.name: Mindhunter
spotlights.spot_it: Two FBI agents and a psychologist interviewing killers in 1970s prisons.
spotlights.story_md: David Fincher's Netflix series, based on John Douglas and Mark Olshaker's 1995 book, followed agents Holden Ford and Bill Tench and psychologist Wendy Carr as they built the Behavioral Science Unit's interview study. Season one (13 October 2017) starred Cameron Britton as Ed Kemper; season two (16 August 2019) moved to the Atlanta child murders. A third season was put on hold in 2020, and in 2023 Fincher said the show was over. Unusually for the genre, it showed the doubts: colleagues questioning whether interviews with a few killers could be turned into rules, and the cost of getting a profile wrong.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most careful screen portrait of how the FBI approach was built.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two seasons, one Kemper, no third act.

spotlights.name: Criminal Minds
spotlights.spot_it: A jet, a whiteboard and a team that names the 'unsub' before the second ad break.
spotlights.story_md: Created by Jeff Davis, Criminal Minds premiered on CBS on 22 September 2005, following the FBI Behavioral Analysis Unit. It ended after 15 seasons in February 2020, was revived on Paramount+ as Criminal Minds: Evolution in November 2022, and its 19th season premiered on 28 May 2026, with a 20th already ordered in March 2026. The real FBI has had to answer the show: its FAQ now explains that it has no job called profiler and that its analysts do not get psychic flashes. A show this long-running has done more to define the word 'profiler' than any study.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Nineteen seasons of near-perfect predictions shape what juries and recruits expect.
spotlights.memory_hook: On TV the profile is always right; that is why it is TV.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Profiling's newest form is not a person but a program. Governments are testing algorithms that score individuals for future violence, and lawmakers are drawing lines around them. The European Union's AI Act, with prohibitions in force from **2 February 2025**, bans systems that predict whether a person will commit a crime based **solely** on profiling or personality traits. In April 2025 documents obtained by Statewatch showed England's Ministry of Justice developing a 'homicide prediction' project. In India, Maharashtra is rolling out AI tools across its police stations, and a June 2025 investigation by Science found the BEOS brain test used in at least 700 cases.

Meanwhile the biggest recent case was closed by DNA and phone data, and the culture keeps returning to profiling's failures: in June 2026 Netflix released two programmes on the Rachel Nickell case. Criminal Minds began its 19th season in May 2026, and John Douglas, aged 80, was billed to speak at CrimeCon in Las Vegas.

spotlights.story_md: Article 5(1)(d) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act prohibits AI systems that assess or predict the risk of a person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics. The prohibitions apply from 2 February 2025. The key word is 'solely': the European Commission's guidelines allow systems that support a human assessment based on objective, verifiable facts directly linked to criminal activity. Critics argue that loophole is large. Supporters say it at least writes into law the principle this whole day has been circling: a profile of who someone is cannot stand in for evidence of what they did.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first major law to ban personality-based crime prediction outright.
spotlights.memory_hook: Europe banned 'he looks the type' when a machine says it.

spotlights.name: England's 'murder prediction' project
spotlights.spot_it: Data on hundreds of thousands of people, fed to algorithms to find future killers.
spotlights.story_md: Through Freedom of Information requests, the group Statewatch found that the Ministry of Justice, working with the Home Office, Greater Manchester Police and the Metropolitan Police, had since January 2023 been developing a 'homicide prediction project', later renamed 'sharing data to improve risk assessment'. Statewatch said the data included people who had never been convicted, including victims, and health markers on mental health, addiction and self-harm. The Ministry said it was research only, using data on convicted offenders, aimed at improving risk assessment. Campaigners called it 'chilling and dystopian' and warned it would encode existing biases in policing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Algorithmic profiling inherits every weakness of the human kind, at scale.
spotlights.memory_hook: From profiling a crime to profiling a population.

spotlights.name: The criminology student caught by DNA
spotlights.spot_it: A PhD student in criminology who studied offenders, convicted by a knife sheath and a white Hyundai.
spotlights.story_md: In November 2022 four University of Idaho students were stabbed to death in Moscow, Idaho. Bryan Kohberger was a criminology PhD student at Washington State University, ten miles away, and his coursework included research on offenders' decision-making. What identified him was not a profile. Cameras caught a white Hyundai Elantra near the house; male DNA on a Ka-Bar knife sheath left at the scene was linked to his family through rubbish collected at their home in Pennsylvania; and his phone went off the network for the two hours around the killings. On 23 July 2025, after pleading guilty, he was sentenced to four consecutive life terms without parole.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most watched case of the decade was solved by forensic data, not behavioural insight.
spotlights.memory_hook: He studied the criminal mind; a snap button on a sheath caught him.

spotlights.name: MahaCrimeOS and AI policing in Maharashtra
spotlights.spot_it: An AI 'copilot' that reads complaints and suggests lines of investigation.
spotlights.story_md: In March 2024 Maharashtra set up MARVEL, a special purpose vehicle with IIM Nagpur and the company Pinaka, to bring AI into policing. Its MahaCrimeOS AI, built on Microsoft's cloud by a partner called CyberEye and aimed first at cybercrime, analyses case information, generates a workflow and suggests investigation pathways, starting in 23 police stations in Nagpur. On 12 December 2025, at its launch with Microsoft, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said it would be extended to all 1,100 police stations in Maharashtra. Government material also describes MARVEL modules that predict likely crime locations. None of the sources found for this day describe an independent audit of its accuracy or bias.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's police are adopting algorithmic analysis faster than they are evaluating it.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Bertillon's cards to a chatbot in every thana.

spotlights.name: The Witness, 2026
spotlights.spot_it: A Netflix drama about the boy who saw his mother killed, and a documentary beside it.
spotlights.story_md: On 4 June 2026 Netflix released The Witness, a three-part drama about the murder of Rachel Nickell, told through her partner Andre Hanscombe and their son Alex, who was two when he saw the attack on Wimbledon Common. Both father and son advised on the series. The documentary The Murder of Rachel Nickell came out the same day. Their release, 34 years after the killing, put the Colin Stagg prosecution, the profile behind it and the missed chances to stop Robert Napper back in front of millions of viewers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Profiling's worst British failure is still being retold.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirty-four years on, the witness tells it himself.

sections.title: How to judge a profile, and the day in brief
sections.intro_md:
Whether you are a juror, a journalist or just watching a documentary, you can test any profile with a few questions. **Is it specific?** 'Male, 25 to 40, has a record' fits most offenders and adds nothing. **Can it be wrong?** A statement that could never be checked is not a prediction. **Is the reasoning shown?** Four in five statements in real profiles came with none. **What is the base rate?** If 90% of offenders of this type already have convictions, saying so is not insight. **Who counted the misses?** A case study listing only hits is an advertisement. **Is it being used to rank, or to convict?** Profiles can help prioritise a list; they should never stand in for evidence.

**The day in brief.** Profiling grew from a dramatic anecdote, the Mad Bomber, into an FBI programme built on 36 interviews. Its famous typology failed its first statistical test, its core assumption of homology failed when measured, and controlled tests show at best a small, uneven edge. Its narrower cousins, geographic profiling, crime linkage and data-driven investigative psychology, make testable claims and hold up better. India shows the darkest form of the idea, profiling by birth, and the newest, profiling by algorithm.

cards.front: Who is this man, and what was his nickname?
cards.back: George Metesky, the Mad Bomber of New York (bombs 1940 to 1956).

cards.front: Who actually found the Mad Bomber's name in 1957?
cards.back: Con Edison clerk Alice Kelly, searching workers' compensation files.

cards.front: Why is Brussel's Mad Bomber profile a weak proof of profiling?
cards.back: It was published before the arrest (the bomber read papers), his memoir dropped wrong guesses (Germany, White Plains), and a file search found him.

cards.front: The two core assumptions of profiling are behavioural ____ and ____.
cards.back: Consistency and homology.

cards.front: What does 'homology' mean in profiling?
cards.back: Offenders who commit crimes in similar ways have similar backgrounds.

cards.front: Name this place and the unit formed there in 1972.
cards.back: The FBI Academy, Quantico; the Behavioral Science Unit.

cards.front: Does the FBI have a job called 'Profiler'?
cards.back: No. Supervisory special agents at the NCAVC do the work, with no 'psychic flashes'.

cards.front: How does racial profiling differ from offender profiling?
cards.back: Offender profiling works backwards from a crime; racial profiling targets people by group before any crime.

cards.front: Whose theory said criminals could be recognised by their bodies?
cards.back: Cesare Lombroso, L'uomo delinquente, 1876.

cards.front: What is this card, and who invented the system?
cards.back: An anthropometric record with mug shots, by Alphonse Bertillon (mug shot standardised 1888).

cards.front: Who wrote a profile of Jack the Ripper in 1888?
cards.back: Police surgeon Thomas Bond, report of 10 November 1888.

cards.front: Who used the word Serienmorder in 1930?
cards.back: Ernst Gennat, head of the Berlin murder squad.

cards.front: What did Walter Langer's 1943 OSS report predict about Hitler?
cards.back: Suicide as the most plausible outcome of defeat.

cards.front: What was the FBI's first active-case profile?
cards.back: Montana, 1973: the Susan Jaeger kidnapping; David Meirhofer was caught after an anniversary phone call.

cards.front: Who is this FBI agent, co-founder of ViCAP?
cards.back: Robert Ressler.

cards.front: Whose 1995 memoir became the Netflix series Mindhunter?
cards.back: John E. Douglas.

cards.front: This nurse researcher helped turn FBI prison interviews into data. Who is she?
cards.back: Ann Wolbert Burgess.

cards.front: How many offenders did the FBI interview for its 1970s to 80s study?
Which talkative killer taught the FBI agents in Mindhunter?
cards.back: Edmund Kemper.

cards.front: Who developed the organized/disorganized split, and when?
cards.back: Roy Hazelwood, FBI, 1980.

cards.front: What did Canter's 2004 test of 100 serial killings find?
cards.back: No distinct organized/disorganized types: organized features were common to most killings.

cards.front: Pinizzotto and Finkel (1990): where did profilers beat the others?
cards.back: On the rape case only; no better on the murder.

cards.front: In Kocsis's tests, which non-expert group did surprisingly well?
cards.back: Science students, who in some tests beat experienced police. Logic seemed to matter more than experience.

cards.front: Snook 2007: profilers' advantage on offence behaviours was r = ____.
cards.back: .00 (overall description .24).

cards.front: Whose 1948 classroom test showed the Barnum effect?
cards.back: Bertram Forer; students rated an astrology text 4.30 out of 5.

cards.front: Alison's two-offender study: what did officers rate the same profile?
cards.back: About 5.3 out of 7, whether matched to the real or a fake offender.

cards.front: Of 880 predictions in 21 profiles, ____% were unsubstantiated.
How accurate was the 1986 FBI case-study profile once all predictions were counted?
cards.back: 38%: 11 right, 18 wrong.

cards.front: Which psychologist questioned personality consistency in 1968?
cards.back: Walter Mischel, Personality and Assessment.

cards.front: Why does Mokros and Alison's 2002 finding matter?
cards.back: Similar crimes did not mean similar offenders, so the homology inference behind profiling failed.

cards.front: Which case does this place recall, and who was wrongly charged?
cards.back: Wimbledon Common, Rachel Nickell (1992); Colin Stagg.

cards.front: Why was Robert Napper ruled out of the Green Chain rapes?
cards.back: He was over six feet tall, a guessed trait used as a filter.

cards.front: These scars are from which 1996 bomb, and who was wrongly suspected?
cards.back: Centennial Olympic Park, Atlanta; Richard Jewell, for 88 days.

cards.front: What does this car show about the 2002 sniper hunt?
cards.back: The Caprice the snipers used; police had focused on a white van and a lone white man.

cards.front: This explosion was blamed on a dead sailor by an FBI analysis. Which ship?
cards.back: USS Iowa, 19 April 1989; Sandia later found an accidental overram.

cards.front: Who was Wearside Jack?
cards.back: John Humble, a hoaxer whose 1979 tape steered the Ripper hunt to Sunderland; jailed 2006.

cards.front: Railway Rapist, 1986: how many of Canter's 17 points did John Duffy fit?
cards.back: 13, by the usual count (some accounts say 12).

cards.front: What identified the Unabomber?
cards.back: His brother David recognised the manifesto's phrasing.

cards.front: What identified BTK in 2005?
cards.back: Metadata on a floppy disk: 'Christ Lutheran Church' and 'Dennis'.

cards.front: Who is this, and what technique caught him in 2018?
cards.back: Joseph James DeAngelo, the Golden State Killer; genetic genealogy.

cards.front: What is distance decay?
cards.back: Offenders commit fewer crimes the further they are from their base, except a buffer zone right around home.

cards.front: Who founded investigative psychology?
cards.back: David Canter, Liverpool.

cards.front: Who developed geographic profiling and the Rigel software?
cards.back: Kim Rossmo, Vancouver police, PhD 1995.

cards.back: The Criminal Tribes Act (1871; 1924 version), which branded whole communities criminal.

cards.front: What is BEOS?
cards.back: Brain Electrical Oscillation Signature profiling, an Indian EEG test claiming to detect 'experiential knowledge'; used in 700+ cases.

cards.front: Which theatre did this writer help found, and with which community?
cards.back: Mahasweta Devi; Budhan Theatre, with the Chhara of Ahmedabad (1998).

cards.front: What did Sukanya Shantha v. Union of India (2024) strike down?
cards.back: Prison-manual rules that assigned work by caste and treated denotified tribes as habitual offenders.

cards.back: AI predicting crime risk based solely on profiling or personality traits, from 2 February 2025.

cards.front: What identified Bryan Kohberger?
cards.back: DNA on a knife sheath, his car on camera and phone data, not a profile. Sentenced 23 July 2025.

quiz.prompt: Guess the case from the clues.

Grand Central Terminal was hit five times.
A psychiatrist's profile predicted a buttoned double-breasted suit.

quiz.prompt: Put these profiling moments in order, earliest first.
Match each offender to what actually identified him.
quiz.explanation: None was identified by a personality profile.

quiz.prompt: Tap the FBI Academy at Quantico.
quiz.explanation: Quantico, Virginia, about 60 km south of Washington, D.C.

quiz.prompt: Tap Wimbledon Common, scene of the 1992 Rachel Nickell murder.
What is this card?
quiz.explanation: Alphonse Bertillon's own anthropometric record: mug shots plus body measurements.

quiz.prompt: This man was one of the FBI's most talkative interviewees. Who is he?
UK officers, 1995: was the share saying they would seek profiling advice again higher or lower than the share calling it operationally useful?
quiz.explanation: 92.4% would seek it again; 82.6% called it useful.

quiz.prompt: The 1986 FBI case-study profile: were its correct predictions higher or lower than its wrong ones?
Which of these makes the narrowest, most testable prediction?
quiz.explanation: Geographic profiling predicts a likely home area, which can be scored. The others are judgements about personality or state of mind.

quiz.prompt: Which of these was NOT barred from compulsory use by the Selvi judgment?
quiz.explanation: Selvi covered narcoanalysis, polygraph and brain-mapping (BEAP). Fingerprinting is ordinary identification evidence.

quiz.prompt: Why do vague profiles feel accurate after an arrest?
quiz.explanation: The Barnum effect: general statements seem specific once you know who they are 'about'.
options: Because profilers see the suspect first
Because juries are told to believe them

quiz.prompt: How did the Wearside Jack hoax damage the Yorkshire Ripper inquiry?
quiz.explanation: Police treated the hoaxer's north-east accent as a trait of the killer and looked away from Bradford.
options: It pointed police to the wrong region and accent
It made police arrest the hoaxer as the Ripper
It contained a false DNA sample

quiz.prompt: John Duffy matched most of the 17 points in David Canter's profile.
quiz.explanation: True: 13 of 17 by the usual count (some accounts say 12). The Railway Rapist case of 1986 was Britain's first major use of a psychologist's profile.

quiz.prompt: A June 2025 investigation found BEOS used in at least 700 Indian police cases.
quiz.explanation: True, reported by Science and ThePrint, despite a 2008 expert panel calling its basis 'suboptimal'.

quiz.prompt: Which picture shows the founder of investigative psychology?
quiz.explanation: Left: David Canter. Right: Walter Mischel, the personality psychologist.

quiz.prompt: What did Sandia National Laboratories conclude about the 1989 USS Iowa explosion?
quiz.explanation: Probably an accidental overram of powder bags, contradicting the FBI-backed suicide theory.
options: An accidental overram of powder bags

quiz.prompt: Match each person to their contribution.
quiz.explanation: Bond 1888, Langer 1943, Burgess from the late 1970s, Rossmo 1990s, Mischel 1968.

quiz.prompt: By the most widely cited estimate, roughly how many people were subject to the Criminal Tribes Act at independence in 1947?
quiz.explanation: About 13 million people in 127 communities. Some historians give much lower figures for those still actively covered.

quiz.prompt: Guess the person.
quiz.explanation: The security guard at Atlanta's 1996 Olympics, suspected for 88 days because he fitted a 'lone bomber' profile.
clues: He found a green backpack under a bench.
He helped clear the area before it exploded.
A newspaper reported he fitted a 'lone bomber' profile.
