quiz_bank.prompt: Who actually found George Metesky's name in January 1957?
quiz_bank.explanation: Con Edison clerk Alice Kelly found his compensation file, marked 'injustice' and 'permanent disability'.

quiz_bank.prompt: According to later research by Donald Foster, Brussel told police the bomber was probably born and educated in Germany.
quiz_bank.explanation: True. Metesky was born in Waterbury, Connecticut, to Lithuanian parents. Brussel's 1968 memoir left that miss out.

quiz_bank.prompt: What is the 'homology assumption' in profiling?
quiz_bank.explanation: Homology: offenders who commit crimes in similar ways have similar backgrounds. Consistency is the separate idea that one offender behaves similarly across his own crimes.
options: An offender behaves the same way in all his crimes
Similar crimes are committed by similar kinds of people
Crime scenes reflect the victim's personality

quiz_bank.prompt: The FBI has an official job title called 'Profiler'.
quiz_bank.explanation: False. The FBI's FAQ says it has no job called profiler; supervisory special agents at the NCAVC do the work.

quiz_bank.prompt: What did Alphonse Bertillon standardise in 1888?
quiz_bank.explanation: The mug shot: a face-on and a profile photograph, alongside his body measurements.

quiz_bank.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
In the 1973 Montana case, a truth-serum interview and polygraph exposed David Meirhofer.
quiz_bank.explanation: False. The polygraph was inconclusive and he was released. A recorded phone call identified his voice.

quiz_bank.prompt: ViCAP, launched in 1985 with Robert Ressler's help, is best described as:
quiz_bank.explanation: A central database for linking unsolved violent crimes across police forces, set up with LAPD's Pierce Brooks.
options: A database for linking violent crimes

quiz_bank.prompt: When Canter's team analysed 100 US serial killings in 2004, what did they find?
quiz_bank.explanation: Organized features were common to most killings and disorganized ones were rare; no distinct two-type split appeared.
options: A clean split into organized and disorganized
Three types: organized, disorganized and mixed
No distinct types; 'organized' features were common to most

quiz_bank.prompt: The organized/disorganized typology was first published after being tested on a large random sample of killers.
quiz_bank.explanation: False. It came from informal interviews with 36 convicted offenders and was tested statistically only later.

quiz_bank.prompt: In Pinizzotto and Finkel's 1990 test, where did FBI profilers clearly beat the other groups?
quiz_bank.explanation: On the rape case. On the murder case they were no better on average.

quiz_bank.prompt: Snook's 2007 meta-analysis: was the profilers' advantage higher or lower for offence behaviours than for the overall description?
quiz_bank.explanation: Overall description r = .24; offence behaviours r = .00.

quiz_bank.prompt: In Forer's 1948 test, where did the 'personal' description each student received come from?
quiz_bank.explanation: Every student got the same text, assembled from a newsstand astrology book. They rated it 4.30 out of 5.

quiz_bank.prompt: When officers compared one profile with a fabricated offender, they rated it as accurate as officers who saw the real offender.
quiz_bank.explanation: True. Both groups averaged about 5.3 out of 7.

quiz_bank.prompt: Walter Mischel's 1968 book challenged which assumption?
quiz_bank.explanation: That people behave consistently across different situations, the trait assumption profiling relies on.
options: That behaviour is consistent across situations
That memory can be read from EEG

quiz_bank.prompt: Mokros and Alison (2002) found that rapists with similar crime-scene behaviour were similar in age, job and record.
quiz_bank.explanation: False. There was no significant relationship, a direct blow to homology.

quiz_bank.prompt: Why did the judge throw out the case against Colin Stagg in 1994?
quiz_bank.explanation: Mr Justice Ognall called the undercover 'honeytrap' operation 'deceptive conduct of the grossest kind'.

quiz_bank.prompt: The D.C. snipers fired from this car while police hunted a white van. What was it?
quiz_bank.explanation: A 1990 Chevrolet Caprice with a firing port cut into the trunk.

quiz_bank.prompt: What finally identified BTK in 2005?
quiz_bank.explanation: Metadata in a deleted Word file on a floppy disk: 'Christ Lutheran Church' and 'Dennis'.

quiz_bank.prompt: The FBI's 1983 replacement profile of the Unabomber, an airline mechanic, led to his arrest.
quiz_bank.explanation: False. His brother David recognised the manifesto's phrasing.

quiz_bank.prompt: In geographic profiling, what is the 'buffer zone'?
quiz_bank.explanation: An area right around the offender's home where he tends to avoid offending, in case he is recognised.
options: A ring around home where offenders avoid striking
The distance a commuter offender travels
A zone of high police patrols

quiz_bank.prompt: Kim Rossmo's 1998 conclusion that a serial killer was targeting women in Vancouver was accepted at once.
quiz_bank.explanation: False. Senior officers rejected it; Robert Pickton was arrested in 2002.

quiz_bank.prompt: When were India's 'criminal tribes' denotified?
quiz_bank.explanation: On 31 August 1952, after the 1924 Act was repealed in 1949. The Habitual Offenders Acts followed.

quiz_bank.prompt: What did the Supreme Court decide in Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010)?
quiz_bank.explanation: Forced narcoanalysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests violate Article 20(3) and Article 21.
options: Forced narco, polygraph and brain tests are unconstitutional
Denotified tribes must register with police

quiz_bank.prompt: How many of the five main Academy Awards did The Silence of the Lambs win?
quiz_bank.explanation: All five: picture, director, actor, actress and adapted screenplay.

quiz_bank.prompt: The FBI's 2008 serial murder report treats 'serial killers are dysfunctional loners' as a myth.
quiz_bank.explanation: True. Many hold jobs and have families; Dennis Rader was president of his church council.

quiz_bank.prompt: The EU AI Act bans AI systems that predict crime based solely on what?
quiz_bank.explanation: Profiling or the assessment of personality traits (Article 5(1)(d)), from 2 February 2025.

quiz_bank.prompt: Bryan Kohberger was identified mainly through a behavioural profile.
quiz_bank.explanation: False. DNA on a knife sheath, sightings of his car and phone data identified him.

quiz_bank.prompt: A profile saying 'the offender is male and probably has previous convictions' is strong evidence of profiling skill for a serial sex offence.
quiz_bank.explanation: False. That is true of most such offenders; it restates the base rate.

side_dish.title: The killer-hunting algorithm that found a cholera pump
side_dish.body_md:
On 31 August 1854 cholera broke out in Soho, London. Physician **John Snow** marked each death on a street map and saw them clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. The parish removed the pump's handle on 8 September, though the outbreak may already have been in decline. His map became a founding image of epidemiology.

More than 150 years later, biologist **Steven Le Comber** at Queen Mary University of London teamed up with **Kim Rossmo**, the policeman who invented geographic profiling. They asked a simple question: if cholera deaths are treated like a serial offender's crimes, can the algorithm find the 'home base'? Using 321 disease sites and 13 neighbourhood pumps, it ranked the Broad Street pump first, in the top 0.2% of the map.

They then tried a live problem: malaria in Cairo. From 139 case locations the model ranked 59 possible water sources. Seven actually held the mosquito Anopheles sergentii, and the model placed six of them in its top six. Field teams had searched almost 300 square kilometres to find those sites.

The same team later fed in the locations of 140 Banksy artworks in London and Bristol. The heat map pointed to places linked to Robin Gunningham, a name first printed in 2008. In March 2026 a Reuters investigation also named Gunningham, which Banksy's lawyer disputed.

The lesson for today's topic: the part of profiling that travels to other sciences is the narrow, testable one, the map, not the mind-reading.

offline_task.title: Write a Barnum profile and test it on a friend
offline_task.body_md:
**Takes 15 minutes, needs one or two people.**

1. Without telling anyone why, write a 'personality profile' of six sentences that could fit almost anyone. Use Forer's tricks: two-sided statements ('At times you are outgoing, at other times you prefer your own company'), flattering ones ('You have a lot of unused potential'), and vague worries ('You sometimes doubt whether you made the right decision').
2. Tell a friend you have been reading about profiling and wrote this about them from how they text or what they wear. Ask them to rate its accuracy from 0 to 5.
3. Now give the same text to a second person and ask the same question.
4. Reveal the trick and talk about it: which sentences felt most 'personal'? Which could actually be proved wrong?

**Then try the opposite.** Write three statements about your friend that *could* be wrong, such as 'You were born in a month ending in -ber' or 'You have never been to Kolkata'. Notice how much harder it is to sound impressive when you can be checked. That gap is the whole scientific problem with personality profiling.

best_facts.fact: The Mad Bomber was not found by the famous profile. A Con Edison clerk, Alice Kelly, found his file because it used the word 'injustice', the same word as his letters to a newspaper.
best_facts.why_surprising: Profiling's founding legend was really a records search.

best_facts.fact: The FBI's own FAQ says it has no job called 'Profiler', and that its analysts do not get 'vibes' or 'psychic flashes' at crime scenes.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most famous job in crime fiction does not officially exist.

best_facts.fact: Police ruled the real killer of Rachel Nickell, Robert Napper, out of an earlier rape series because he was over six feet tall.
best_facts.why_surprising: A guessed physical trait let a serial attacker walk free.

best_facts.fact: When officers were shown one profile alongside two completely different 'offenders', both groups rated it equally accurate, about 5.3 out of 7.
best_facts.why_surprising: A profile can seem to fit whoever is arrested.

best_facts.fact: A celebrated 1986 FBI profile made 29 predictions; only 11 were right, a 38% hit rate, yet it was published as a success.
The organized/disorganized typology, still taught worldwide, failed when tested on 100 US serial killings in 2004: no two types appeared.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most famous profiling idea was never validated before it spread.

best_facts.fact: BTK asked police whether a floppy disk could be traced. They replied in a newspaper ad, 'Rex, it will be ok', and the disk's metadata named his church and 'Dennis'.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 30-year hunt ended because a killer trusted the police's tech advice.

best_facts.fact: By the most cited estimate, India's Criminal Tribes Act covered about 13 million people in 127 communities at independence, presumed criminal by birth.
best_facts.why_surprising: Profiling by birth was the law for 78 years.

best_facts.fact: In some of Kocsis's profiling tests, science students picked for their logical reasoning outscored experienced police officers.
best_facts.why_surprising: Logic beat years on the job.

best_facts.fact: Ten of 14 American Psychological Association experts rejected the FBI analysis that blamed sailor Clayton Hartwig for the USS Iowa blast; engineers later pointed to an accident.
best_facts.why_surprising: A psychological autopsy convicted a dead man in public.

best_facts.fact: Geographic profiling, built to find serial killers, ranked the Broad Street pump first of 13 pumps in John Snow's 1854 cholera data.
best_facts.why_surprising: A crime tool solves an epidemic retroactively.

best_facts.fact: Students in Forer's 1948 class rated a 'personal' description 4.30 out of 5. All had the same text, copied from an astrology book.
India's BEOS brain test has been used in at least 700 cases, though its main validation study, of 110 people, was never peer reviewed.
best_facts.why_surprising: Unvalidated neuroscience is steering real investigations.

best_facts.fact: The Wearside Jack hoax tape may have delayed the Yorkshire Ripper's arrest by 18 months; police had interviewed Sutcliffe nine times.
best_facts.why_surprising: One fake clue outweighed nine real interviews.

best_facts.fact: Berlin's Ernst Gennat used the word Serienmorder in 1930, decades before 'serial killer' became an FBI term.
best_facts.why_surprising: A famous American coinage has a German ancestor.

best_facts.fact: By the 2020s only two full-time behavioural investigative advisers were supporting all of Britain's police forces.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 'profiler' profession is tiny outside fiction.
